title: Krishna Embraces His Old Friend
story:
Sudama had walked a long road to reach this gate — all the way from his poor village to the king's palace in Dwaraka — carrying nothing but four handfuls of flattened rice tied in a rag. Years before, he and Krishna had been schoolboys together, studying at their teacher's house. Now Krishna was a king, and Sudama was so poor that this small bundle was the only gift he could bring. He stood at the palace gate and knew he was out of place.

The palace of Krishna housed sixteen thousand queens, and the building that held them was a city of its own — courtyards and corridors, gardens and lamps, guards who had seen every kind of man come and go but who looked at the ragged brahmana and saw something they could not place. But no one turned him away, and no one asked his business, as though the palace itself were waiting for him.

Sudama did not have to wonder what to do next. From somewhere deep inside the palace, Krishna saw him — saw him from afar, through rooms and walls and the whole long passage of years since they had been boys together. He rose from the couch where he sat with Rukmini and hurried to the gate — the king of Dwaraka, running to meet a guest in rags.

He embraced him. The tears came to Krishna's eyes — the old texts say it plainly: the tears of joy — as he held his old friend, the best of brahmanas, thin and weary from the road. Sudama, who had feared he might not even be recognized, found himself wrapped in his friend's arms. Krishna held him a long moment, and when he drew back his hands stayed on Sudama's shoulders, as if he could not quite believe the road had brought him.

Krishna would not let him stand. He took him by the hand and seated him on his own couch. And then the servants of the palace could scarcely believe what their eyes reported: the king himself knelt and washed the feet of the ragged guest, and took the water and bore it to his own head, honoring it as the holiest of things. In all the palace, no one moved; the servants stood frozen, watching their king serve his guest. He had fragrant incense brought and rows of lamps lit, and he received his friend with joy, as though a treasure had come to the palace rather than a poor man. A poor man's gift, a king's welcome — somewhere between the two, the old friendship simply resumed.

The women of the inner palace saw it, and the wonder of it stopped them where they stood. Krishna, whose fame was spotless, whose word held the worlds together, had seated a penniless brahmana on his own couch and washed his feet with his own hands. They had seen kings bow to him and learned men worship him; they had never seen him honor anyone like this. "What good deed has this man performed," they whispered to one another, "that our king should cherish him so — a man with nothing, while the queen of fortune herself serves him?"

Rukmini herself came and stood beside them, and took up a fan, and fanned the weary brahmana — she, the goddess of fortune, cooling the man who had arrived at her palace with nothing but a rag of flattened rice.

And the two friends sat and talked. Not of kingdoms, not of wealth. They talked of the old days, of the years when they had studied together in their teacher's house — the mornings, the lessons, the small adventures of boys — and the palace around them, for all its splendor, faded to nothing next to that.

The women of the palace watched the king of Dwaraka sit and talk and laugh with a guest who had arrived in rags, and they understood — many of them for the first time — what kind of king they served.
reflection: The palace women's question — what merit has this beggar performed? — is the story's hinge. By every worldly measure Sudama deserves nothing, yet Krishna honors him as a treasure. The episode turns the usual logic of honor upside down: the king bows to the poor man, and the goddess of fortune fans him, because friendship, not rank, is what the lord of Dwaraka counts.
next_story_tease: Then Krishna asked what gift his old friend had carried all the way from home.
hero_scene: Krishna, risen from his couch, embracing the emaciated, ragged Sudama with tears on his face, while Rukmini stands beside them with a fan and the women of the palace look on in astonishment.
